notable_anecdotes.description: Yearly since 2017, FLP -- with Tan Yan Kee Foundation and Ayala Corporation -- awards P200,000 scholarships to at least 20 law students, plus a dissertation writing contest: P320K first prize, P220K second, P120K each for three third prizes, P20K each for up to 20 finalists, P100K-P50K faculty adviser honoraria.
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Concrete program scaffold preserving the financial structure for the historical record.

notable_anecdotes.description: Jay-em Cuntapay's first-prize dissertation challenged the concept of 'Viral Sovereignty,' arguing that a virus 'should not be treated as a genetic resource over which states may assert sovereign rights' -- a position with direct implications for vaccine access during the pandemic.
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Highlights the topical relevance and ambition of the scholarship.

notable_anecdotes.description: William Christian Dela Cruz (FSUU Butuan), speaking for the 21 new scholars: 'How is the law felt on the margins? ... closing the borders of communities where the poor live for a long period of time without giving them adequate assistance is a life-and-death matter.'
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Captures the moral throughline of the column -- law as experienced from below.

notable_anecdotes.description: Snippets from four scholar essayists -- Omamalin on reciprocal liberty, Ramos on the co-equal throne of economic justice, Pacumio on the rule of law as 'the great equalizer,' Laza on the roots metaphor of remaining grounded -- each from a different Philippine university (USC, U Cordilleras, UST, SLU Baguio).
notable_anecdotes.purpose: Geographic and institutional diversity demonstrating reach of the program beyond Metro Manila.

one_paragraph_summary: Writing as Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity (FLP) chair after the week's awards ceremony, CJ Panganiban honors the 2021 scholars and dissertation winners by yielding the column space to their own voices. He opens by restating the program scaffold -- yearly since 2017, FLP with the Tan Yan Kee Foundation and Ayala Corporation awards at least 20 P200,000 scholarships and the dissertation writing contest (P320K/P220K/3 × P120K/up to 20 × P20K finalists, P100K-P50K adviser honoraria) -- and frames the awardees as the future presidents, lawmakers, Cabinet members, governors, mayors, justices, and judges of the country. The bulk of the piece quotes the scholars themselves: Jay-em Cuntapay (ADMU, first prize) on challenging 'Viral Sovereignty,' Eunice Baliong on free trade in essential medical equipment, Catherine Lim on biotechnological inventions, Trisha Dulanes on reinterpreting freedom of thought against Brain-Computer Interface evils, Noelle De Vera on Chinese FDI; William Christian Dela Cruz (FSUU Butuan), speaking for the 21 new scholars, on how law is 'felt on the margins' during pandemic border closures that are 'a life-and-death matter' for daily-wage earners; and Jani Omamalin (USC) on reciprocal liberty, Paula Ramos (U Cordilleras) on economic justice 'on the same throne' as civil and political rights, Daverick Pacumio (UST) on the rule of law as 'the great equalizer,' and Cecilia Laza (SLU Baguio) on the roots metaphor of remaining grounded. The column closes by pointing readers to www.libpros.com for full copies. It reads as both donor-stewardship report and generational manifesto in the scholars' own words.
